interest: Japan's licensing rules for foreign doctors and the U.S. barrier to reciprocity.
overview: This file from the State Department decimal file 894.1281 covers regulations and individual inquiries concerning the practice of medicine, surgery, dentistry, and optometry by foreigners in Japan between 1931 and 1933. The earlier portion of the file concerns an inquiry by Dr. Tetsuya G. Ishimaru, an American practitioner in Los Angeles seeking State Department assistance to obtain an optometry license in Japan; the Department concluded that it could not intervene because medical licensing was an internal Japanese administrative matter and reciprocal recognition was impossible due to medical licensing in the United States being controlled by individual states rather than the federal government. The later portion contains Despatch No. 374 from U.S. Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmitting an official note from Japanese Foreign Minister Count Yasuya Uchida and a detailed memorandum from the Japanese Ministry of Home Affairs outlining the annual examination procedures, fees, language options (English, German, or Japanese), theoretical and clinical subjects, and required application forms on mino-gami paper for foreign medical and dental candidates, noting that British subjects remained exempt by treaty while Mexican exemptions had ceased following the abrogation of their bilateral treaty in 1928.

subfiles.about: Japanese Foreign Office note and Home Ministry memorandum detailing procedures, fees, subjects, and forms for foreign medical licensure examinations.
subfiles.summary: Foreign Minister Count Yasuya Uchida responds to Ambassador Grew's inquiry, announcing that the Department of Home Affairs has decided to permit foreign applicants to take medical and dental examinations in English or German as well as Japanese. The appended Home Ministry memorandum sets forth comprehensive regulations: applicants must have completed over four years in a foreign medical school, cannot have certain criminal convictions or physical disabilities, must apply annually in December with a 15-yen revenue stamp, and must sit for theoretical and clinical examinations held annually in Tokyo. It also provides prescribed application and curriculum vitae templates to be written on traditional mino-gami paper.
subfiles.title: Note from Foreign Minister Uchida with Home Ministry memorandum on foreign medical examinations
